meta.title: Lalbaugcha Raja
meta.location: Lalbaug Market / Putlabai Chawl area, Lalbaug, Mumbai
meta.foundedNote: 1934 is corroborated by institutional materials, municipal history and reporting; 12 September is a retrospective exact date.
meta.intro: Lalbaugcha Raja is the Lalbaug Market festival of Lalbaugcha Raja Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Mandal, founded in 1934. Its widely remembered origin concerns fishermen and traders seeking a permanent market. Devotees know the idol as Navsacha Ganpati, associated with vows. The royal sculptural form and Kambli family are important to its modern identity, while evidence also preserves other makers and pandemic interruptions. It is separate from Ganesh Galli’s Mumbaicha Raja.

sections.title: A market and a community vow

paragraphs.text: A municipal tourism history recounts the 1932 closure of the Peru Chawl market and the fishermen’s and traders’ wish for a permanent place to work. It describes the September 1934 idol as an act of gratitude, dressed as a fisherman. This is an attributed devotional origin account, not a demonstration that a supernatural intervention caused the land grant.

Ramu Ramanathan’s 2017 history gives 12 September 1934 as the first installation and describes local intermediaries negotiating with the landlord. Marathi reporting also associates the 1934 foundation with the Koli community’s vow. Nearby Ganesh Galli has a separate 1928 institution; its foundation, artists and giant-idol milestones must not be transferred to Lalbaugcha Raja.

sections.title: The Kambli legacy and other makers

paragraphs.text: The Kambli family’s association is remembered from 1935 and remains central to the contemporary idol. It was not necessarily an exclusive, uninterrupted monopoly. In a 2026 interview, Manohar Bagwe recalled the Bagwe family’s 1990-1996 commissions; the report also lists other makers in particular years. These retrospective assignments should remain attributed until matched against mandal records.

sections.title: An interruption preserved in institutional records

paragraphs.text: The mandal’s Arogyautsav page records a 2020 programme of blood/plasma donation and assistance. Indian Express reports no installed idol in 2020, a four-foot idol in 2021, and restoration of public visits in 2022. The health programme was a changed form of collective service; it should not be illustrated with an undated usual-size idol as if nothing changed.

The institution also lists medical, educational and disaster-relief work outside festival worship. The two contemporary photographs included here document a 2023 procession scene and the 2025 physical pandal. They establish specific moments, not the age of a sculptural mold or an unbroken annual appearance extending back to 1934.

Six scanned stage photographs retain printed festival years: 1967, 1968, 1972, 1974, 1977 and 1978. They show changing court and narrative settings around Ganesh. The present gallery supplies no individual HTML year captions, so other numeric files are not dated by sequence. Original negatives, print dates, processing and credits remain unresolved.

sections.title: Changing tableaux before a familiar royal image

paragraphs.text: The official historical gallery preserves photographs, devotional portraits and treated prints together. Item-level printed years establish several attributions that the gallery's numeric filenames cannot. Its physical stage photographs show Ganesh among civic figures in 1969, in a Mirabai scene in 1971, and in social and epic narratives in 1975-1979. These objects document changing display practice, while their negatives and later print treatment remain unverified.

A 1976 print supplies the explicit sculptor credit Manohar Raghunath Chavan, and the 1979 print credits Chandrakant Kambli. These positive item-level records complement later artisan interviews. They do not establish an exclusive maker for every intervening year. Colour-treated 1950 s prints and the isolated 1937/1940 portraits remain separately classified.
